chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
title: Hines and McShann treated as footnotes to Armstrong and Parker; Michael's Pub
summary: Both are asked mainly about others; Dance describes McShann being buried at Newport and helping him at Michael's Pub.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Well, I can't really blame him for that because that is an insult, you know.
It's kind of almost like telling a good man, all I know about you is some other guys went on from you.

Well, I mean, the thing about Louis is -- I mean, nobody wants to take any credit from Louis. But I mean, for goodness sake, Earl Hines himself was an innovator. It happened that they worked together. Then when he went back with Louis because he was in bad shape financially -- that was the only reason he went with Louis again, now everybody seems to think that -- or almost think he's a A lot of them anyway. Dixieland player. And, you know, he doesn't know how to handle that, you know.
He can't say to them, well, don't you realize. all I am is who I am. He can't say that, you know.
That could be a hidden thing, especially to one of the pioneers.

But I think the same thing does apply to McShann, because as you say, all they want to talk about is the fact that he brought Charlie Parker to New York. That ridiculous. Because, I mean, you listen to him on some of these things -- he made this new record recently when he was here, and he, you know, not only plays well, but he swings more than anybody. You know, picks up immediately and starts playing.
Yeah, he's just -- I always try to console him. I tell him, it's coming, it will be here. You think 12 years ago, they wouldn't hardly let you back in New York.
Well, you know, I got him to come into that. I told George Wein to bring him into that, Newport Festival. And, you know, they just buried him. I mean, he hardly was heard.

Then another time when he came in here with Claude Williams, Claude Williams buried him, and that was his own fault. But this time, playing in Michael's Pub, the (unintelligible) said, would I talk to the guys, because he wanted to hear McShann's piano and McShann's singing. So, you know. I talked to Buddy Tate, Quinclette and Milt Hinton and Jack
Williams, and they understood. But it was really very good. I mean, I'm not taking any credit for it, but Jay himself wouldn't have said anything.
